Script block

Source: R/script-block.R
new_script_block.Rd

A block whose state is an ordinary R script. The script reads its inputs by name and returns whatever its last statement evaluates to: a data frame for the blocks downstream, a ggplot, a gt table, or any other object.

Usage

new_script_block(
  script = "n <- 6\n\nutils::head(data, n)",
  values = list(),
  ...
)

Arguments

script

R code, either a single string with embedded newlines or a character vector of lines, which is joined with \n.

values

Named list of current control values, restored with a saved board. Values for names the script no longer declares are dropped.

...

Two arguments are read here, and the rest is passed to blockr.core::new_block().

  • starters: the scripts "Start from" offers in the editor, as a list of list(label, hint, script), where hint may be left out. NULL, the default, keeps the built-in ones.

  • class: classes to put in front of script_block, for a block built on this one.

Neither is part of the block's state, which is why they are not named arguments: blockr.core saves every named argument of a constructor. A restored block gets both from its constructor again.

Value

A block of class script_block.

Details

A script that does not parse, or that has no statement returning a result, still gives a block, with a warning. The block then shows that reason as its error. A saved board that holds such a script loads, and the script can be repaired in the editor.

Inputs

The block takes any number of inputs, including none.

  • The first link into the block is data. A script written for one input reads data, as it would in a function.

  • Every link also reads by its own name: the link name, or .arg1, .arg2, ... for a link that has none. Only the links without a name are counted, so next to one named link the first unnamed one is .arg1. Links are named where they are drawn: "Edit link" or "Edit inputs" in the dock.

  • The block is variadic (function(id, ...args)), so the order of the links decides which one is data. A link that is removed and drawn again comes last, and data is then another input. A script with more than one input should read each by its own name, which does not move. A link named data is always data.

  • With no input connected, data is NULL and the script is a source: it reads a file, calls an API or builds a data frame itself.

On export each input name is replaced by the id of the upstream block, so the exported code reads like a script someone wrote by hand.

Controls

A top-level assignment whose right-hand side is a plain value becomes a control on the block, meaning a literal, a c() of literals, or a call to factor() or as.Date(). Everything else is code.

.vars <- intersect(c("AGE", "SEX", "TRT"), names(data))  # private, no control

vars <- factor(.vars, levels = .vars)                # a multi-select
species <- factor("setosa", levels(data$Species))    # a dropdown
n <- 10                                              # a number box
desc <- TRUE                                         # a checkbox

data |>
  dplyr::filter(Species %in% species) |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = n)

A factor is how a select is expressed: its levels are the choice list, and the length of its value decides single or multiple. For a text column write sort(unique(data$col)) as the levels. unique() alone follows the order of the rows, and the control is drawn again whenever that changes. A pick whose level is no longer in the data is not used: the control goes back to the value the script wrote.

A name starting with a dot is never a control. A name the script assigns again is not one either, since only the last assignment could be.

The script reads a control as its current value, written into the code as a literal. Three things follow, all by design:

  • A select's pick is a string (a character vector for a multi-select), not a factor. levels(x) or as.integer(x) on a control do not give what they give for the factor on the declaration line.

  • Every read of the control's name is replaced, also inside data-masking calls. With a control n, dplyr::filter(n > 5) compares the control and not a column called n. Write .data$n for the column. .env$n does not reach the control: its line is no longer in the code that runs.

  • A later declaration reads an earlier control at its current value, so the choices of one dropdown can depend on the pick in another: col <- factor("SEX", names(data)) followed by val <- factor(character(0), sort(unique(data[[col]]))).

The optional #| annotation carries what a value cannot say, such as a numeric range or a label: n <- 10 #| number(min = 1, max = 50).

Sentence

#| title:, #| subtitle: and #| caption: lines give the block a sentence whose words are its controls, as blockr.viz's blocks do:

arm <- factor("Placebo", levels = sort(unique(data$TRT01A)))
top_n <- 8  #| number(min = 3, max = 15)
serious <- FALSE  #| label = "serious events only"
#| title: Top {@top_n} adverse events in {@arm}
#| subtitle: Subjects per term[, {@serious}]

{@arg} prints a control's value and makes the word clickable: a select opens its list, a number or text becomes a field, a checkbox toggles. A clause in [ ... ] leaves when its value is empty, and its control is offered as a + label chip instead.

label_off gives the chip its own text. A checkbox's word is its label, so label can say what is shown and label_off what a click adds:

all_pts <- TRUE  #| label = "including all patients column", label_off = "Add all patients column"
#| ui_subtitle: [{@all_pts}. ]

On, the subtitle reads including all patients column.; off, it shows the chip + Add all patients column. A chip's tooltip and ARIA label carry the same text. Any control takes label_off, for the chip it gets when its value is empty.

{n}, {label(col)} and {col} read the first input, as the data frame sentence_data() makes of it. The sentence sits in the row with the gear; the controls it names leave the grid, the others stay. A date can be named but stays a control in the grid. The sentence is shown above any result and is not part of the exported code.

Exported code

The current values are written into the body as literals, so the exported code has no assignment left for a control.

blockr.core fills the input names in with bquote(), which also evaluates every .() and ..() the script calls itself, such as data.table's .(x). Write list(x) there. The editor footer names the line.

Saved as lines

A saved board writes the script as a JSON array, one element per line, so a change to the script shows up in a git diff as the lines that changed.

Building on the script block

Another package can build a block on this one. Its constructor calls new_script_block() with a class, its own default script and, if it likes, its own starters:

new_listing_block <- function(script = "my_listing(data)", values = list(),
                              ...) {
  blockr.script::new_script_block(
    script, values,
    starters = my_starters(),
    class = "listing_block",
    ...
  )
}

The block has the classes c("listing_block", "script_block", "block"), so every method of the script block applies to it. A saved board restores it through new_listing_block(), which therefore takes script, values and ..., no other named argument, and passes ... on. Register the constructor with blockr.core::register_blocks() as any other block.

The constructor is found by its arguments: it is the nearest function in the chain of calls that takes exactly script, values and .... It may therefore reach new_script_block() through a helper of its own. Where there is no such function, as for new_script_block(class = "x") called at top level, the block is saved with a constructor that keeps the class and the starters it was built with.

What such a block draws is decided by the class of the script's result, not by the class of the block: see block_result_output(), result_head() and result_titles(). For an input that is not a data frame, see sentence_data().

Examples

blk <- new_script_block("n <- 6\n\nutils::head(data, n)")

# the same script, one element per line
blk <- new_script_block(c("n <- 6", "", "utils::head(data, n)"))

# no input: the script is the source
blk <- new_script_block("data.frame(x = 1:3, y = c(\"a\", \"b\", \"c\"))")

if (interactive()) {
  library(blockr.core)
  serve(
    new_board(
      blocks = c(
        a = new_dataset_block("band_members", package = "dplyr"),
        b = new_dataset_block("band_instruments", package = "dplyr"),
        s = new_script_block("merge(data, instruments, by = \"name\")")
      ),
      links = links(
        from = c("a", "b"),
        to = c("s", "s"),
        input = c("data", "instruments")
      )
    )
  )
}
